title: Optimal Navigation on Simplicial Complexes
authors: Diego Febbe, Duccio Fanelli, Gianluca Peri, Timoteo Carletti
abstract: The navigation time and optimal search strategies deriving from random dynamical processes on binary graphs have been extensively explored and analyzed, being of prominent interest in the network science field. In this work, we study an extension of these topological measures for simplicial complexes: a specific type of geometric and algebraic structures that encapsulates higher-order interactions. Here, the explorability analysis of simplicial complexes has been conducted in terms of the mean first passage times between nodes, i.e. the 0th-order simplices, with the inclusion of a long-range stochastic teleportation term modulated with respect to the local random walk hopping across the various dimensions. We also provide a perturbative approximation scheme recovering the modulation parameter between pure random walk and teleportation mode (for higher-order setting) acting as the expansion parameter.
summary: This paper analyzes optimal search strategies by extending random walk concepts from simple graphs to higher-order simplicial complexes. It models the dynamics as a mix between local movement and global jumps, using mean first passage times. The key finding is that optimizing search efficiency requires a specific, non-trivial balance ($\alpha \in (0, 1)$) of these two processes in complex structures.
main_problem: The work extends topological measures, such as navigation time and optimal search strategies, from simple binary graphs to simplicial complexes to account for higher-order interactions.
main_result: For simplicial complexes, the minimum mean exploration time occurs at an intermediate modulation parameter $\alpha \in (0, 1)$, suggesting that optimal searching requires a balance between local random walks and global teleportation, unlike simple networks.
method: The analysis uses mean first passage times calculated via matrix inversion ($Z_j = I - R_j$) and employs a perturbative approximation scheme in the modulation parameter $\alpha$ to study the asymptotic behavior of the search process.
model_or_system: The system is modeled on simplicial complexes, which are geometric/algebraic structures capturing multi-body interactions. The dynamics are governed by a modified random walk operator $R = \alpha M + (1 - \alpha) D_s S$, where $M$ represents local hopping and $S$ represents global teleportation.
key_observables: Mean first passage times ($\langle T \rangle$), normalized occupation frequency, and the optimal modulation parameter $\alpha$.
important_parameters: The modulation parameter $\alpha$, which controls the balance between local random walk dynamics ($M$) and global stochastic teleportation ($S$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on a perturbative expansion in $\alpha$ (truncated initially) and assumes that simulation time is much larger than the Fiedler time for asymptotic results.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate examples of higher-order networks, the random walk process across dimensions, and plots showing how the mean exploration time ($\langle T \rangle$) varies as a function of the modulation parameter $\alpha$, contrasting network vs. simplicial complex behavior.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the mathematical framework by generalizing random walks to higher-order structures (simplicial complexes). It then develops methods using connection matrices and mean first passage times, culminating in an analysis of how the optimal search strategy ($\min \langle T \rangle$) depends on the mixing parameter $\alpha$.
why_interesting: While focused on network science, the mathematical tools developed—analyzing dynamics across structured state spaces (simplicial complexes) using spectral methods and perturbation theory—are highly relevant to modeling complex many-body systems or emergent collective behavior in condensed matter.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

Fig. 4: Here we show how the number of structures in the simplicial complex can be counted as a function of the degree of lower-dimensional simplices. In panel (a), we see how the number of links is counted once for each connected node. In panel (b), we see that the degree of the link [0, 1] can be counted as the sum of the two lower-dimensional structures (nodes 0 and 1) plus the number of incident upper connected triangles.
